near_miss.lead: Conditional oath: divine favour for truth, anger for falsehood
near_miss.why_not: The context invokes God and all his saints. Searches for hollur, Latin propitius and Greek perjury forms found ordinary favourable-god prayers (Cato Agr. 134.2, 139.1, 141.2) and a conditional oath in Andocides De mysteriis 98 s4, but no distinctive cognate collocation. The slab partner is a chronicle report of thunder, not an oath; gramur means angry here. Neither shared inherited wording nor independence from Christian oath tradition is established.

near_miss.lead: Putting prescribed words into another person’s mouth
near_miss.why_not: The Norse contexts describe coaching a speaker. The Latin slab partner concerns the moon and terrestrial creatures; the other partners do not reproduce the expression. Searches combining word and mouth material found Norse speech idioms, including Christian material, but no cross-branch counterpart with the same lexical and syntactic structure. A negative search is not proof of absence.

Norse kasta with orðum is an insult metaphor. The Atharvan partners use nud- for driving away hostile entities; ónýtum here means useless and cannot supply the pushing verb. A Homer search for βάλλω with speech words found Il. 15.566, inwardly taking a saying to heart, not attacking someone with words. The predicates are not cognate and the actions differ.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_2_11_Agathangelos ed. page 1429 - PDF page 135 (word id 23655) (w2/3)
near_miss.why_not: Close reading and a two-root corpus search confirm anatomical co-occurrence but not a common figure. Harald rests on his own knees and elbows while warming himself; Euripides has the speaker put her arms at another person’s knees in supplication; Bhīma uses knee and elbow against an opponent. The syntax, participants and action differ. The Armenian sea passage is a false lexical hit, and later Greek geometric/anatomical hits do not establish a formula.

near_miss.lead: Abandoned human body as food for birds and beasts
near_miss.why_not: Grágás requires covering a corpse to prevent scavenging. Odyssey 3.271 concerns abandoning a singer as prey for birds, but does not share the Norse eating predicate or bird noun; the paired Iliad 17.151 speaks of prey for Argives. The image alone cannot anchor an inherited wording claim. Corpus search found closer eating-predicate parallels outside the slab, recorded separately as a search lead.

near_miss.lead: Life and property merism: fjörs and fjár
near_miss.why_not: Grágás describes the capacity to fight and defend one’s life and property. Its slab partners do not share the merism. Searches for livestock with man/hero found Atharvan paśu-/vīra- and Avestan pasu-/vīra- pairings, but fjör means life, not man/hero, and is not the second cognate in that equation. The property noun alone does not establish inherited wording; the alliterating Norse legal pair may be a Germanic formation.

near_miss.lead: Going to one’s father / going to the Fathers
near_miss.why_not: The Norse scenes concern visiting a living father or returning home. AVŚ 18.2.s95 directs the dead to the ancestral Fathers by Yama’s path. Even where come/go and father are cognate, the number, referent, destination and ritual context differ. Norse fund is a meeting in these phrases; its distant etymological relation to a path does not make the phrase an ancestral-road formula.

Odyssey 9.367 coordinates the speaker’s mother and father. The Norse pivot identifies Sveinn’s mother and then her father, Atli: two generations, not the same parental pair. Shared kinship nouns do not establish the same merism.

near_miss.lead: Naming witnesses compared with Sanskrit name formulas
near_miss.why_not: The recurrent Norse legal instruction appoints witnesses to a declaration. The Sanskrit passages state names or the collective designation for wives; they do not appoint witnesses or attest a declaration. The name root and ordinary speech context supply no distinctive inherited legal collocation.

search_lead.cognate: Norse eti (éta, present subjunctive plural) and Greek ἔδονται / ἔδοιεν continue the eating root *h₁ed-. Norse dýr and fuglar are not cognate with the Greek scavenger nouns.
search_lead.argument: Grágás prescribes covering a dead man so that beasts and birds will not eat him. The Homeric passages, checked with adjacent lines, imagine dogs and vultures eating a fallen enemy. Both combine terrestrial and avian scavengers as subjects of a cognate eating predicate with a human victim. Norse generalizes the animal categories and reverses the desired outcome in a legal burial requirement. Worth further review as possible continuity of a traditional image with lexical renewal, but ordinary scavenging realities and the medieval Christian legal setting remain serious alternative explanations; this is not an established inheritance claim.

error.correct_reading: Haraldr, personal name, accusative singular; mark as name.
error.evidence: The preposition introduces Harald Grey-cloak, with the personal epithet following. Mapping the name to troops and ruling does not make these lexical predicates in the passage.

error.correct_reading: Sveinn, personal name, genitive singular; mark as name.
error.evidence: The following genitive konungs identifies King Sveinn; this is not a reflexive expression from *swé.

given_etymon.gloss: root: to shake, tremble; to fear, be afraid

error.correct_reading: Bhīma, nominative singular masculine personal name.
error.evidence: Bhīma is the agent of the attack in this scene, not a free adjective expressing fear or trembling.

given_etymon.gloss: root: to cut; to split, to separate

error.evidence: Valda governs the dative: ability to wield a shield is coordinated with shooting a bent bow. This is not the verb skilja, separate.

given_etymon.gloss: root: to set in motion; to flow

error.correct_reading: danskr, feminine nominative singular adjective Danish, agreeing with tunga; remove the asserted flow-root mapping.
error.evidence: The expression names the Danish language. The mapped *dʰonh₂is/flow entry does not identify this ethnonymic adjective.

error.correct_reading: ónýtr, dative plural adjective useless; retain the use/benefit analysis, remove the pushing-root alternative.
error.evidence: It modifies words characterized as worthless in an insult exchange. The use/benefit base nýtr is distinct from the Atharvan pushing verb that generated the apparent comparison.
